source.title: Self-Play Pretraining with Zero Data
source.authors: Aditya Cowsik; Kfir Dolev; Michael Y. Li; G. DeLuca; Nourya Cohen; Noah D. Goodman; Yoav Levine

record.file_problem: No apparent garbling or truncation; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests compute-scaling of held-out prediction loss in a new training setting—zero-data self-play—and across several modalities.
record.gate_note: Table 2 reports fitted compute-scaling exponents for ten datasets; these are recorded separately below. The paper also compares self-play with fixed-universal-prior and PCFG pretraining, stating that the former scales substantially more slowly and that PCFG benefits vary by domain. These comparisons are not assigned dataset-level rows here because the supplied text gives their results only in plots, without separately stated values. The paper’s ICL results are not rows for downstream predictability: they vary the number of in-context examples, not model scale or pretraining loss.
record.test_reason: The study fits compute-optimal frontiers L(C)=E+AC^-b to zero-shot natural-data loss of models pretrained only on self-play synthetic program outputs, across ten datasets in several modalities (Table 2). Its own results bear on whether the power-law form holds in a new training regime with transfer evaluation (V5). The loss is not held-out loss on the pretraining distribution, so it does not bear directly on V1.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly right but should add a point. The authors also claim self-play exponents are comparable to, if slightly higher than, published natural-data exponents. They cautiously read this as suggesting that universal structure accounts for much of natural-data scaling gains.
record.recipe_differences: The study fits compute-optimal loss frontiers, but trains randomly initialized models through adaptive self-play on synthetic program outputs and evaluates zero-shot on held-out datasets; it does not reproduce standard natural-data language-model scaling experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The compute-optimal frontier varies model size, checkpoint/training duration, and ensemble size. Hyperparameters are tuned separately by scale using validation loss averaged across DCLM and DNA; the paper notes limited natural-data leakage through hyperparameter selection.
record.problems: The experiments are confined to models below 25M parameters and a 4K context. The fitted scaling exponents in Table 2 have no reported uncertainty. Hyperparameter selection uses natural validation data, although the authors state that natural data are not used for gradient updates.
record.rows_left_out: The paper includes additional per-dataset loss curves in Figures 1, 2, and 7, and comparisons with fixed-universal-prior and PCFG pretraining. These plotted results are not separately rowed because the supplied text does not provide dataset-specific numeric values for them; the explicit compute exponents in Table 2 are recorded above.

untested.parts: No held-out loss on the training distribution is reported; all losses are zero-shot transfer to natural data. Isolated parameter or token scaling is not reported.
No held-out extrapolation from small to much larger runs.
No fitted growth of optimal N and D with compute.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
Models are below 25M parameters, over roughly 1e15–1e19 effective compute. Repeated data and fine-tuning scaling are not tested; the pre-pretraining experiment in A.1 uses one model size.
ICL results vary the number of demonstrations, not scale or loss.
Fitting and setup choices are not varied. The comparison with literature exponents is not a fit-dependence test.

missing.what: Compute-scaling frontiers for the fixed universal-prior and PCFG pretraining baselines. These are plotted only; the universal prior is described as scaling substantially more slowly.
Frontiers on additional datasets (Common Crawl, Kolmogorov text, arXiv math, Speech Commands, ESC-50, MusicNet, LibriSpeech, CIFAR planar, glibc rand, arithmetic), plotted without fitted exponents

record.verdict_notes: The literature exponents in Table 2 are cited values, partly derived from Chinchilla-form fits, and should not become rows. Hyperparameters were tuned on DCLM and DNA validation loss. Training used a constant LR, so checkpoints stand in for shorter runs. The frontier ends where no lower-loss models were found, suggesting saturation at the top of the compute range. The reader linked rows to V1; I restricted them to V5 because the evaluated loss is transfer loss, not held-out pretraining loss.

versions.untested_parts: Tests compute scaling along compute-optimal frontiers, not isolated parameter-count or token-count scaling with the other quantities held non-bottleneck; does not establish the law for larger models.
Does not report a held-out extrapolation test in which fits on small runs predict runs orders of magnitude larger.
Constructs compute-optimal frontiers over model sizes and checkpoints, but does not report stable power-law growth of optimal parameter and token counts with compute or compare their exponents.
Does not compare depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.

Tests self-play transfer across the reported image, audio, speech, music, text, code, DNA, and formal-math datasets. Does not test repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer across larger-scale models.
Does not test whether downstream task performance improves predictably with scale or pretraining loss; its ICL evaluation varies the number of demonstrations.
Does not systematically vary parameter-count conventions, fitting methods, training schedules, or data choices to test how scaling exponents or allocation laws depend on them.
